BENECON312.name: Econometrics

BENECON312.topics: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? analysis: The technical option develops Python, databases, software construction in C++ and Haskell, design and evaluation of algorithms, calculus, linear algebra, probability, numerical modelling, vision, machine learning, agent planning and deep and reinforcement learning. Computer vision moves to an available spring after programming. The unchanged set would overfill spring offerings, so Networks & Operating Systems adds infrastructure, resource management and concurrency where the closest option previously had a second empirical methods course. Statistics & Experimental Methods retains research design and modelling. The health option retains programming, data, modelling, AI and vision while adding epidemiological reasoning, anatomy, physiology, advanced pathophysiology and health psychology. Meta-analysis and econometrics supply separate evidence synthesis and causal-methods contributions without implying medical or clinical training. The cognitive option retains psycholinguistics after the brain and behaviour gateway and places neural networks, search and learning in the final semester. Perception, attention, language, philosophical inquiry and robotics relate human and machine intelligence without claiming a dedicated UX studio. The pairwise differences are nine, eight and ten courses (67.5, 60 and 75 EC). Robotics supports motion planning and manipulation but does not sustain a distinct embedded-systems pathway. AI planning and numerical work contribute to logistics and simulation without a separate operations or supply-chain progression. The educational minor requires subject didactics and school practice. Alignment credits the vision elective once and distinguishes partial NLP, graph, simulation and operations research coverage from a full dedicated course. Maastricht’s 18 EC thesis is required and the separate UCR research opportunity is optional.

alignment.rationale: Both introduce data analysis. UCR develops data preparation, visualisation and analysis in R. Maastricht also introduces intelligent agents and search.
Both teach control flow and functions. UCR uses Python and Maastricht uses Java.
UCR introduces object-oriented programming within its first programming course. Maastricht offers a separate course in Java.
Both develop requirements, design, testing and code review. UCR practises software development in C++ and Haskell.
Both develop discrete mathematical reasoning, logic and proof.
Both develop differentiation and integration. UCR also applies differential equations to modelling.
UCR covers logic within discrete mathematics. Maastricht offers a separate formal logic course.
Both cover systems of linear equations, matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations.
Both cover numerical methods for roots, integration and differential equations. UCR also studies interpolation and algorithm accuracy.
Both study dynamic models, including transfer functions and state-space representations. UCR focuses on linear signals and systems.
UCR introduces linear programming within optimisation. Maastricht devotes a course to linear programming.
Both study algorithms and data structures. UCR includes experimental analysis of algorithm performance.
UCR studies graph algorithms within algorithms and data structures. Maastricht has a separate graph theory course.
Both teach SQL and relational databases. UCR covers normalisation, authorisation and query processing.
UCR covers sampling, experiments and statistical inference. Maastricht uses data-science methods to study inference from observational and experimental data.
Both study distributions, estimation and statistical inference. UCR also uses computer algebra for simulation.
UCR uses simulation in probability and statistics. Maastricht has a dedicated course in simulation and analysis of its outputs.
Both fit statistical models to data. UCR approaches modelling through experimental research.
Both cover classification, regression and clustering. UCR evaluates model performance using practical data.
UCR uses neural networks for text classification and introduces large language models. Maastricht has a dedicated natural language processing course.
Both study image processing and computer vision. UCR builds a recognition pipeline and tests it on new images.
Both develop search and constraint-solving techniques. UCR includes optimisation and search in adversarial settings.
Both address constrained decisions under uncertainty. Maastricht also covers dedicated operations research methods.
